meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Dying is Easy. Comedy is Hard'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Kean. The deathbed line traces to actor Edmund Gwenn, first printed in 1966; the terse wording was popularised by the 1982 film My Favorite Year.

answer.label: Not Edmund Kean — traced to Edmund Gwenn
answer.sourceLine: Edmund Kean died in 1833, and Quote Investigator ↗ reports that it has “not located any solid support” for crediting him. The earliest published account QI has found is from 1966, and it is about a different actor entirely — Edmund Gwenn, whose deathbed reply to the director George Seaton was first printed as “Not nearly as difficult as playing comedy.” The neat modern wording arrived decades later, and QI concludes the exact phraseology “may be lost.”

source.excerpt:
“All this must be terribly difficult for you, Teddy.”
“Not nearly as difficult as playing comedy.”
trail: 1833 — Kean dies, and the line is nowhere. Edmund Kean made his last stage appearance at Covent Garden on 15 March 1833, playing Othello to his son Charles’s Iago, broke down mid-scene, and died a few weeks later in Surrey. Wikipedia’s article on Kean ↗ still states that “his last words were alleged to have been ‘dying is easy; comedy is hard’” — sourcing it to Jeffrey Kahan’s The Cult of Kean (Ashgate, 2006), a book published long after the story was already circulating in print.

1966 — the story surfaces, about someone else. The first published description Quote Investigator has located ↗ is in Act Your Way to Successful Living by Neil and Margaret Rau, where the dying actor is Edmund Gwenn and the reply is “Not nearly as difficult as playing comedy.”

1974–76 — Jack Lemmon carries it into circulation. Seaton told the story to Lemmon, who retold it in a Los Angeles Times profile of 27 January 1974 (“But it’s not as bad as playing comedy”) and again in Don Widener’s 1975 biography Lemmon, where “bad” has become “hard.” Walter Kerr repeated Widener’s version in The New York Times on 10 September 1976, as Barry Popik documents ↗.

1982 — the movie fixes the wording, and the wrong name. Peter O’Toole’s Alan Swann delivers the compressed line in My Favorite Year and presents it as a dying actor’s last words. Weeks later, in The New York Times of 14 November 1982, Carl Reiner offered “It was Edmund Kean, I think” and Larry Gelbart corrected him on the spot — both quoted by Popik ↗.
source.excerptNote: This is George Seaton’s account of his last visit to Gwenn at the Motion Picture Country House, as retold by Neil and Margaret Rau in 1966 — “Teddy” was Seaton’s nickname for him. Note what is not here: the famous seven-word version. The whole anecdote turns on a single comparison, and the crisp “dying is easy” framing was added by later retellers. Quote Investigator ↗ notes that the Raus’ version and the two later versions told by Jack Lemmon all differ in precise wording.

source.rightsNote: No status can honestly be asserted here. This exact seven-word wording cannot be tied to any pre-1931 work: the earliest account of the underlying anecdote that Quote Investigator located ↗ is a 1966 book that phrases it quite differently, and the best-known instance of the terse form is dialogue in the 1982 film My Favorite Year, which remains in copyright to its screenwriters and studio. Because the adage’s wording evolved anonymously across retellings, there is no identifiable first publication of this sentence to assign a public-domain date to — so we claim none.

author.name: Edmund Gwenn
author.kicker: The actor with the best claim
author.heading: Who was Edmund Gwenn?
author.metaLine: 1877–1959 · English stage and screen actor; Academy Award winner
author.bio: Born Edmund John Kellaway in Wandsworth, London, Gwenn spent years at the Court Theatre under J. E. Vedrenne and Harley Granville-Barker, where he played Straker, the chauffeur in Bernard Shaw’s Man and Superman, before Hollywood remade him as a character star. He won the Academy Award for Best Supporting Actor as Kris Kringle in Miracle on 34th Street (1947), took a second nomination for Mister 880 (1950), and turned up in four Alfred Hitchcock films. He died of pneumonia in Woodland Hills, California, on 6 September 1959, twenty days short of his eighty-second birthday — which is where this story begins.

misattribution.heading: Everyone it has been pinned on
misattribution.intro: This is a floating adage: it attaches itself to whichever great actor the teller admires most, and it always arrives as last words. The pattern is diagnostic — a line that keeps changing whose deathbed it was said on is a line nobody wrote down at the time.

items.why: Quote Investigator ↗ states plainly that it “has not located any solid support for this attribution.” The claim is nonetheless repeated on Kean’s Wikipedia page ↗ as his “alleged” last words, cited to a 2006 book — long after the anecdote was already in print about someone else.

items.who: Peter O’Toole as Alan Swann, My Favorite Year (1982)
items.why: The 1982 Richard Benjamin comedy, written by Norman Steinberg and Dennis Palumbo, is where most people have actually heard the line — O’Toole plays the dissolute matinee idol Alan Swann ↗. Wikipedia’s Kean article records that O’Toole “delivered the line … and attributed it to the last words of Kean.” It is a scripted joke about show-business folklore, not a citation.

A Chicago Tribune feature of 6 September 1975 ran the identical bedside exchange with Crisp as the dying man — same retirement home, same punchline — and even hedged that “the story may be apocryphal,” as Quote Investigator documents ↗.
Both names circulate, but Quote Investigator ↗ is blunt about them: “the evidence is non-existent.”

misattribution.truthLine: The most that can honestly be said: on George Seaton’s testimony, Edmund Gwenn did say something like this as he was dying in 1959 — but the recorded versions differ, and Quote Investigator concludes ↗ that “the exact phraseology may be lost.” The seven words everyone quotes are a polish applied by later tellers.

context.heading: Why the wrong name stuck
lead: Two English actors named Edmund: one famous for tragedy, one famous for playing Santa Claus. The mix-up almost writes itself — and the wrong Edmund is the more flattering one, because a line about comedy being harder than dying lands with far more force from the man who collapsed on stage playing Othello than from the star of Miracle on 34th Street. Attribution drifts toward whoever makes the better story.

The correction has been public for a long time and simply hasn’t taken. When The New York Times convened comedy writers in November 1982 to talk about the line from My Favorite Year, Carl Reiner offered Kean and Larry Gelbart put him right in the next breath. That exchange has been on the record since 1982, and Kean’s encyclopedia entry still carries the claim.
context.detailsSummary: There is a real, much older line about comedy being serious — and it isn’t this one
detailsBody: If you want a genuinely antique version of this sentiment, it belongs to David Garrick, not Kean. Thomas Campbell’s Life of Mrs. Siddons (1834) has Garrick warning the young John Bannister off comic parts: “you may humbug the town for some time longer as a tragedian; but comedy is a serious thing, so don’t try it yet.”

Even that comes with a caveat. Quote Investigator points out ↗ that Campbell was writing many years after Garrick’s death in 1779, “hence, its credibility is reduced.” And note what the old version does not contain: any mention of dying. The deathbed framing — the part that makes the modern line quotable — is a twentieth-century addition.
context.pull: “In the first place, that’s wrong. It wasn’t Edmund Kean, it was Edmund Gwenn.” — Larry Gelbart, 1982

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator states it has "not located any solid support" for attributing the maxim to Edmund Kean (1787–1833); names Groucho Marx and Stan Laurel as further credits where "the evidence is non-existent"; identifies the earliest located publication as Neil and Margaret Rau, Act Your Way to Successful Living (Prentice-Hall, 1966), pp. 145–146, giving Edmund Gwenn's reply to George Seaton as "Not nearly as difficult as playing comedy"; cites the 27 Jan 1974 Los Angeles Times Jack Lemmon profile (p. O21), the 6 Sept 1975 Chicago Tribune piece crediting Donald Crisp (which says "the story may be apocryphal"), Don Widener's 1975 book Lemmon (p. 184), and the 1982 film My Favorite Year; and concludes "the exact phraseology may be lost."

Barry Popik's entry reproduces the 10 September 1976 New York Times piece by Walter Kerr retelling the Gwenn/Seaton story ("But not as hard as playing comedy"), and the 14 November 1982 New York Times piece by Fred Ferretti in which Carl Reiner says "It was Edmund Kean, I think" and Larry Gelbart replies "In the first place, that's wrong. It wasn't Edmund Kean, it was Edmund Gwenn"; it also quotes Ralph Keyes's Quote Verifier verdict, "Invented 'last words' making the show business rounds."

Wikipedia's Edmund Kean article states "His last words were alleged to have been 'dying is easy; comedy is hard.'" citing Jeffrey Kahan, The Cult of Kean (Ashgate Publishing, 2006), p. 2; states that Peter O'Toole "delivered the line, 'dying is easy; comedy is hard' and attributed it to the last words of Kean in the 1982 movie My Favorite Year"; gives Kean's dates as 1787–1833; and records his last stage appearance at Covent Garden on 15 March 1833 playing Othello to his son Charles's Iago, when he broke down mid-scene, after which he died a few weeks later in Surrey.

Wikipedia's Edmund Gwenn article gives his name at birth as Edmund John Kellaway, dates 26 September 1877 – 6 September 1959, birthplace Wandsworth, London; records his work at the Court Theatre under J. E. Vedrenne and Harley Granville-Barker including Straker in Shaw's Man and Superman; his Academy Award for Best Supporting Actor for Miracle on 34th Street (1947); a second Academy Award nomination for Mister 880 (1950); appearances in four Alfred Hitchcock films; and his death from pneumonia after a stroke in Woodland Hills, California, twenty days before his 82nd birthday. The current article contains no mention of the "comedy is hard" line or of his last words.

This Internet Archive item is a borrowable copy of Ralph Keyes, The Quote Verifier: Who Said What, Where, and When (St. Martin's Press, 2006) — the reference work cited by both Quote Investigator and Barry Popik on this saying.

Quote Investigator's separate article on "comedy is a serious thing" traces it to David Garrick's advice to John Bannister as reported in Thomas Campbell's 1834 Life of Mrs. Siddons — "you may humbug the town for some time longer as a tragedian; but comedy is a serious thing, so don't try it yet" — and notes that Campbell wrote "many years after the death of Garrick in 1779; hence, its credibility is reduced." The article contains no mention of Edmund Kean.

Wikipedia's My Favorite Year article confirms the film is from 1982, directed by Richard Benjamin, written by Norman Steinberg and Dennis Palumbo from a story by Palumbo, released by Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer, with Peter O'Toole as Alan Swann. (The article itself does not quote the "dying is easy" line; that detail is sourced instead to Wikipedia's Edmund Kean article and to Quote Investigator.)
